## Proof

**Claim:** $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^k X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}\;\middle|\;\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m\right] = \dfrac{k}{n}.$

**Step 1: Exchangeability is preserved under conditioning.**

Since $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are i.i.d., their joint distribution is exchangeable: for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, $(X_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, X_{\sigma(n)})$ has the same distribution as $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$.

The conditioning event $\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m\right\}$ is symmetric in $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ — it is invariant under every permutation $\sigma$. Therefore the conditional distribution of $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ given $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m$ remains exchangeable.

**Step 2: Equal conditional expectations.**

By exchangeability of the conditional distribution, for every pair $i, j$:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_i \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[X_j \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right].$$

Denote this common value by $\mu$. By linearity of conditional expectation:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\!\left[X_i \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \;\middle|\; \sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right] = m.$$

Hence $n\mu = m$, so $\mu = \dfrac{m}{n}$.

**Step 3: Compute the target conditional expectation.**

Since $m > 0$ (a positive integer), the denominator $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m$ is a positive constant under the conditioning, so we may pull it out:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}\;\middle|\;\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m\right] = \frac{1}{m}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^k X_i \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right].$$

By linearity and Step 2:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^k X_i \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right] = \sum_{i=1}^k \mathbb{E}\!\left[X_i \;\middle|\; \textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_\ell = m\right] = k \cdot \frac{m}{n} = \frac{km}{n}.$$

Therefore:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}\;\middle|\;\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m\right] = \frac{1}{m} \cdot \frac{km}{n} = \boxed{\dfrac{k}{n}}.$$

**Remark.** The result is independent of both the common distribution of the $X_i$ and the value of $m$. The only ingredients are: (i) i.i.d. (hence exchangeable) structure, (ii) the symmetry of the conditioning event, and (iii) $m > 0$ so the denominator is a well-defined positive constant.
